title: Sigala, alone
tomorrow: the Kalamas have heard too many teachers. how do they decide?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha's last word in DN 16: everything made comes apart; strive on. Today, a sutta about everyone who's still here.

Early morning outside a city. A young man named Sigala, hair and clothes still wet, is bowing: east, south, west, north, down, up. The Buddha, walking in for alms, asks him why. Sigala says his father told him to, as he was dying. He doesn't know what it's for. He just keeps the promise.
screen: `WET HAIR, BOWING AT DAWN.` → `EAST, SOUTH, WEST, NORTH, DOWN, UP.` → `HIS FATHER TOLD HIM TO.`

segments.voice: The Buddha doesn't tell him to stop. He fills the directions in. In paraphrase: east is your parents. South, your teachers. West, your partner and children. North, your friends. Below, the people whose work supports you. Above, those who teach the spiritual life. Then the surprise of DN 31: every direction runs both ways. Children care for their parents; parents keep children from harm and teach them a skill. Students show up for teachers; teachers train them well and introduce them to good friends. Friends keep their word and stay in hard times; the people who work for you are treated fairly and given rest. So a bow turns into a map of everyone holding up your life, and of what you owe each of them. Now look back at the week's road. She chose. The direct path. Sixteen steps. A mind like the earth. The wheel. Strive on. Six lines, and today, six directions to carry them in.
screen: `THE BUDDHA FILLS THE DIRECTIONS IN.` · `PARENTS, TEACHERS, FAMILY, FRIENDS.` · `EVERY DIRECTION RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · `A MAP OF WHO HOLDS UP YOUR LIFE.` · then, large: `SIX DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Pick one direction: a parent, a teacher, a friend, someone whose work supports yours. Bring one person from it to mind, and one small duty you owe them. Sit with that person in view, as if bowing toward them.
Sigala: the young man of DN 31, whose dawn bow to six directions the Buddha turned into a map of the people in his life.
Six directions to carry home, and each one bows back to you. Two weeks of reading, gathered.

howItsDone: The Sigalovada Sutta is taught in Theravada communities as guidance for lay life, and its six directions are often used to talk about family, school, friendship and work.

what a scholar hears: DN 31, the Sigalovada (or Singalovada) Sutta, sometimes called the householder's discipline; the Buddha reinterprets an inherited rite instead of abolishing it.

Sigala.meaning: a young householder who bowed to six directions at dawn

DN 31.meaning: the Sigalovada Sutta, advice to a householder

DN 16.meaning: the sutta of the Buddha's last journey and passing

alms.meaning: food given to monks, who walk to collect it

notes: DN 31 paraphrased: Sigala (Singalaka), wet hair and clothes, worships the six directions at his dying father's word; the Buddha, entering Rajagaha for alms, explains the noble way: east parents, south teachers, west wife and children, north friends, nadir servants/workers, zenith ascetics and brahmins; reciprocal duties for each. The script gives a few duties per pair, not the full lists. Confirm.
'West, your partner and children' modernizes 'wife and children'; the sutta's duties run between husband and wife. Confirm the phrasing.
'Above, those who teach the spiritual life' renders 'ascetics and brahmins'; confirm.
The middle sections (the vices, false and true friends) are left out for length; the outline's practice 'do one duty' becomes a sit with one duty in view.
